lesson.title: Compose matrix maps

steps.headline: A B means do B first, then A. Entry (i, j) of A B is row i of A dotted with column j of B.

lead.text: Applying one map and then another is composing them. The matrix of the composed map is the product A B.
A B v means A(B v). The inner matrix acts first, and the order of the two matrices matters.
The expression A B v is short for A(B v).

reveal.text: You read it from the inside out. In a product of maps, the matrix nearest the vector acts first.

steps.headline: Compare A B v with B A v for A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, B = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 1).

workedSteps.text: Swap the order. A acts first, then B.

steps.headline: Find entry (1, 2) of A B, for A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: Entry (1, 2) uses row 1 of A, which is (1, 2), and column 2 of B, which is (0, 3).
Dot the row with the column. What is the entry?

lead.text: Let A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$. Entry (2, 1) pairs row 2 of A with column 1 of B.

reveal.text: You paired a row of A with a column of B and added the products. That is the rule for every entry of a product.

lead.text: Matrix A holds the prices of 3 products in 2 shops, so it is 2 × 3. Matrix B holds the sales of those 3 products in 2 months, so it is 3 × 2.

lesson.orientation: Multiply compatible matrices and keep the order of composition.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Machine P doubles a number and machine Q adds 3 to it. You start with 5. In one run you use P and then Q. In another you use Q and then P.

intro.promise: By the end you'll multiply two matrices entry by entry, and say which map acts first in a product.

recap.keyIdea: A matrix product is two maps in a row, and B acts first. Swap the order and the result usually changes. Entry (i, j) is row i of A dotted with column j of B.

blocks.text: You found that entry (1, 2) of A B is 6 while the reversed product gives 4, and that a 2 × 3 matrix times a 3 × 2 matrix gives a 2 × 2 matrix.

recap.nextHook: Some maps can be undone. Next: the identity matrix, and when an inverse exists.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: First run: 5 × 2 + 3 = 13. Second run: (5 + 3) × 2 = 16. The difference is 3.

questions.prompt: How much bigger is the final number of the second run than the first?
hints: Work out each run in full.
In the first run, double 5 and then add. In the second, add and then double.
Subtract the first run's answer from the second's.

misconceptions.feedback: The two orders do not give the same number. Calculate each run in full.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Doing the same two operations in a different order gave different results. That is why the order of a matrix product matters.

acceptedIdeas: Row 1 of A with column 1 of B
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Row i of A with column j of B, here with i = 1 and j = 1.

questions.prompt: To find entry (1, 1) of A B, which row and column do you pair?

choices.label: Row 1 of A with column 1 of B
Row 1 of B with column 1 of A
Column 1 of A with row 1 of B

hints: The left matrix gives the row. The right matrix gives the column.

misconceptions.feedback: That reverses the order. The left matrix gives the row and the right matrix gives the column.
Rows of the left matrix pair with columns of the right matrix, not the other way round.

questions.onCorrect: Entry (i, j) of A B is row i of A dotted with column j of B.

questions.prompt: Which map acts first in A B v?
hints: Read the expression from the inside out.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: B acts first, since A B v means A(B v).

misconceptions.feedback: A acts on the result of B v, so it comes second. The matrix nearest v acts first.

questions.onCorrect: A B v means A(B v). The matrix next to v acts first.

acceptedIdeas: Each map acts on the output of the other, so the order changes what it acts on.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In one order B gets v, and in the other B gets A v. Different inputs, different outputs.

questions.prompt: Why do A B v and B A v give different results?

choices.label: Each map acts on the output of the other, so the order changes what it acts on.
Matrix multiplication only works one way round.
The vector v changes between the two.

hints: Compare what the second map receives in each case.

misconceptions.feedback: Both products exist here. They are just different matrices.
The vector v is the same. What changes is what each map receives.

questions.onCorrect: Each map receives a different input in each order, so the results usually differ.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (1, 2) of A B? Count from 1.
hints: Pair the first row of A with the second column of B.
Multiply matching positions, then add.
The row is (1, 2). Dot it with the column.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses column 1 of B. The question names column 2.

questions.onCorrect: Row 1 of A dotted with column 2 of B: 1 × 0 + 2 × 3.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (2, 1) of A B? Count from 1.
hints: Use the second row of A and the first column of B.
Multiply matching positions, then add.
One of the products involves a zero.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the second column of B. The question asks for the first.

questions.onCorrect: Row 2 of A dotted with column 1 of B: 1 × 1 + 0 × 2.

questions.prompt: A is 2 × 3 and B is 3 × 2. What is the shape of A B?
hints: Keep the outer numbers and drop the matching inner ones.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 2 × 3 times 3 × 2 gives 2 × 2: the inner 3s match and vanish.

misconceptions.feedback: That would use the inner numbers. They match and disappear; the outer numbers stay.
That is the shape of A. The product has A's rows and B's columns.

questions.onCorrect: The inner 3s match and vanish. A B has A's rows and B's columns: 2 × 2.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (1, 2) of B A? Count from 1.
hints: B is now the left matrix, so it gives the row.
Pair the first row of B with the second column of A.
Multiply matching positions, then add.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first row (2, 0) and second column (2, 1) give 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the same entry of A B. In B A, matrix B goes first.

questions.onCorrect: Row 1 of B dotted with column 2 of A: 2 × 2 + 0 × 1.

questions.prompt: Which identity holds for any matrices A and B that can be multiplied?
hints: Transposing a product reverses the order of its factors.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: (A B)ᵀ = Bᵀ Aᵀ: the order reverses.

misconceptions.feedback: That keeps the order. Transposing reverses it, like taking off shoes and socks.

questions.onCorrect: A transpose reverses a product: the last factor's transpose comes first.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (2, 2) of A B? Count from 1.
hints: Use the second row of A and the second column of B.
Multiply matching positions, then add.
The row is (2, 1). Dot it with the column.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses column 1 of B. The question asks for column 2.

questions.onCorrect: Row 2 of A dotted with column 2 of B: 2 × 1 + 1 × 2.
